You said:

A stock closed at $80. But after hours bid/ask is at $70. What does this mean?

ChatGPT said:

I’ll explain the mechanics and the practical implication, not assume a specific ticker. The key distinction is “official last close” versus “current after-hours quotes.”

It means: the official regular-session close was $80, but the current after-hours market is pricing it closer to $70.

Think of it this way:

Close at $80 = last regular-hours trade around 4:00 PM.

After-hours bid/ask around $70 = after the close, the best available buyers/sellers are now around $70.

So the stock is indicating a roughly 12.5% drop after hours:

(70−80)/80=−12.5%(70 - 80) / 80 = -12.5\%(70−80)/80=−12.5%

But important nuance:

A bid/ask at $70 does not always mean many shares traded at $70. It may mean the current quote is there. After-hours trading has lower liquidity, fewer participants, wider spreads, and more volatile/uncertain prices than regular trading, according to SEC and FINRA risk disclosures. SEC+1

Practical interpretation:

If the quote is bid $69.50 / ask $70.50, the market has likely repriced the stock down after news, earnings, guidance, offering, dilution, lawsuit, etc. It may open near $70 tomorrow if that price holds.

If the quote is bid $70 / ask $85, that is not a clean “$70 price”; it is a wide, illiquid spread. A market order could get ugly.

If there are almost no trades, the quote can be misleading or temporary.

The safest mental model: $80 is yesterday’s official close; $70 is the current after-hours indication. The stock has not “officially closed” at $70, but the market is currently leaning there.

Also: avoid market orders after hours. Use limit orders only, because spreads and liquidity can be bad.

ChatGPT said:

Your intuition is mostly right: selling at $70 and immediately buying back at $70 does not create trading profit. The only thing it changes is your tax/accounting position and execution risk.

Right — selling at $70 and buying back at $70 does not create profit.

You would be doing this:

  1. You bought at average cost: $66.02

  2. You sell at: $70

  3. Profit realized: $3.98/share

  4. Then you buy back at: $70

  5. You still own DRAM again, but now your new cost basis is around $70

So economically, you did not “make extra money.” You just converted your unrealized gain into a realized gain and re-entered at the same price. In a taxable brokerage account, that may create a tax bill, because the IRS says selling above your adjusted basis creates a capital gain. IRS

The only way selling helps is if you sell at $70 and buy back lower, say $62. Then you avoided an $8/share drop. But if you sell at $70 and buy at $70, no benefit.

On your second point: yes, if your plan is truly long-term, buying more on drops can make sense — but only if your thesis and position sizing still make sense. DRAM is not a broad S&P 500 ETF. It is a concentrated memory/AI ETF; Roundhill currently shows Micron, SK Hynix, Samsung, and Kioxia as the biggest holdings, with Micron + SK Hynix + Samsung alone making up a large majority of the fund. Roundhill Investments

One important correction:

If your average cost is $66.02, then buying at $70 does not average you down. It averages you up.

Buying at:

  • $70: increases your average cost, but may still be fine if you believe long-term upside is much higher.

  • $66: roughly keeps average similar.

  • $60: averages you down.

  • $50: averages you down a lot, but maybe because something serious changed.

So I would think about it like this:

Long-term bullish and position is small: do not panic sell; consider staged buys on drops.

Long-term bullish but position is already large: hold, but do not keep adding blindly.

Not sure about the ETF / bought because it was running up: reduce risk instead of “averaging down.”

A clean approach:

Keep the current shares. Do not sell at $70 just to buy back at $70.
Decide a maximum total dollar amount you are comfortable having in DRAM.
Add only in stages, for example at $70, $65, $60, not all at once.

That is basically dollar-cost averaging: investing set amounts over time instead of trying to perfectly time one entry. Investor.gov describes this as a way to manage timing risk by following a consistent pattern over a long period. Investor.gov

The dangerous version is: “It dropped, so I must buy more.”
The better version is: “I have a long-term thesis, a max position size, and predefined buy levels.”


You said:

Whats stop loss vs stop limit

ChatGPT said:

A stop-loss and a stop-limit both start with the same idea:

“Do nothing now. But if the price falls to my trigger price, activate a sell order.”

The difference is what kind of sell order gets activated.

1. Stop-loss / stop-market

Example:

DRAM current price: $80
Stop price: $77
Quantity: all shares

Meaning:

“If DRAM hits $77 or lower, sell immediately at the best available market price.”

So if DRAM slowly drops:

$80 → $79 → $78 → $77

Your order triggers and you may sell around $76.90–$77.00.

But if DRAM gaps down:

$80 → opens at $70

Your order triggers, but the available market price is now around $70, so you may sell near $70, not $77.

Stop-loss = better chance of getting out, but sale price is not guaranteed.

2. Stop-limit

Example:

Stop price: $77
Limit price: $76.50
Quantity: all shares

Meaning:

“If DRAM hits $77, activate a sell order — but only sell if I can get at least $76.50.”

If DRAM slowly drops to $77, you might sell around $76.50–$77.

But if DRAM gaps straight to $70:

Your stop triggers, but your limit says:

“Do not sell below $76.50.”

Since buyers are around $70, your order may not sell at all. You keep holding DRAM.

Stop-limit = protects your minimum sale price, but you may fail to exit.

Simple comparison

OrderYour commandMain benefitMain risk
Stop-loss / stop-market“Sell if it falls below $77.”More likely to exitCould sell far below $77
Stop-limit“Sell if it falls below $77, but not below $76.50.”Avoids terrible fillMay not sell at all

Plain English

Stop-loss:
“Get me out if this breaks down.”

Stop-limit:
“Get me out if this breaks down, but only at a price I approve.”

For your DRAM case:

If your priority is I do not want to hold if it crashes, use stop-loss / stop-market.

If your priority is I refuse to sell below a certain price, use stop-limit.

But there is no order that guarantees both:

“Sell for sure, but also guarantee me $77.”

That is the key thing.
